long.title: Why a Dim Blue Lamp Beats a Blinding Red One — the photoelectric effect | Bear's Notes
long.description:
Aim the brightest red lamp you own at a metal plate — and not one electron escapes. Swap in a dim blue glow, and electrons fly off the instant it lands. Crank the red lamp up to blinding, pour on more and more light — and still, nothing.

A Brown Blue explainer, in the 3Blue1Brown tradition: concrete before abstract, mystery before formula.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:22 The wave picture breaks
0:37 Light as packets
0:52 The escape cost
1:03 Near-misses and clean hits
1:26 E = hν — the photon
1:52 The mystery dissolves
2:06 Sodium, by the numbers
2:23 What we skipped, and your turn

In this video: why a blinding red lamp frees no electrons while a dim blue one works instantly; light arriving as packets whose energy is set by color alone (E = hν); the all-or-nothing escape cost Φ; the leftover K = hν − Φ and the threshold frequency; and sodium by the numbers — where 300 nm succeeds and a ten-thousand-watt green lamp fails.

Source: Quantum Mechanics, Vol. 1, Ch. 1 — Why Classical Physics Failed.
